title: I Tried to Fool a Scientific Publisher With AI
gist: IEEE Spectrum writer Benjamin Skuse used free ChatGPT/Gemini and then Analemma's autonomous FARS system to produce two papers for IEEE Access; integrity checks caught both, via ghost citations and heavy preprint reliance respectively. The piece quantifies the AI-slop flood (57% of 2025 papers show LLM influence) and argues detection is a losing arms race, pushing publishing toward provenance and reproducibility checks.

themes.theme: Scale of AI slop in journals

insights.claim: An estimated 57% of academic articles published by 2025 showed detectable evidence of LLM influence, up from 12% in 2023.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: LLM use in scholarly writing went mainstream in roughly two years.
insights.quote: By 2025, an estimated 57 percent of all published academic articles exhibited detectable evidence of large language model (LLM) influence, a massive jump from 12 percent in 2023.

insights.claim: Over 12% of Nature Communications peer reviews in 2025 were found to be completely AI-generated.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: AI has penetrated the review side, not just authoring.
insights.quote: over 12 percent of Nature Communications reviews were found to be completely AI-generated in 2025

insights.claim: Only about 1 in 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI use in 2025 formally disclosed it, implying measured AI involvement is grossly understated.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Disclosure-based policies capture a tiny fraction of actual AI use.
insights.quote: for every 40 papers showing statistical evidence of AI usage in 2025, only one formally disclosed it

insights.claim: Some estimates put fake, often AI-generated, academic publications at hundreds of thousands per year.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Fraud volume is now industrial-scale.
insights.quote: some estimates suggest that hundreds of thousands of fake, often AI-generated, publications are now produced annually

insights.claim: IEEE's research-integrity manager argues AI slop threatens not just the scientific record but trust in science as a whole.
insights.speaker: Amanda Sulicz
insights.so_what: Integrity failures could become a systemic credibility problem for science.
insights.quote: AI slop is completely eroding trust in science and every scientific process that we’ve worked for centuries to create.

insights.claim: A non-expert using only free ChatGPT and Gemini produced a superficially plausible, IEEE Access-formatted fake optics paper in roughly two dozen prompts without editing any output.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: The barrier to producing convincing fake papers is near zero.
insights.locator: Two Ways to Make a Paper

insights.claim: Model guardrails were easily bypassed: when one LLM refused, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like 'hypothetically' often worked; Gemini was more willing than ChatGPT to generate synthetic studies.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Cross-model switching defeats single-vendor safety refusals.
insights.quote: If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick.

insights.claim: The forged paper was caught by automated integrity checks for hallucinated 'ghost citations': STM Integrity Hub flagged 12 and a MolecularConnections checker could not validate 24 references.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Reference validation is currently the most effective automated tripwire against naive AI fakes.
insights.locator: As it turned out, I was

insights.claim: Stylistic AI tells such as hedging, triplet lists, and formulaic transitions are weak detectors because unimaginative human writers use them too; the forgery contained no 'tortured phrases'.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Style-based AI detection has poor precision.
insights.quote: these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too

insights.claim: An optical-soliton expert found the forged paper professionally written but flagged excessive acronyms and a couple of confidently stated, debatable physics claims.
insights.speaker: Gaetano Assanto
insights.so_what: Domain experts remain needed to catch subtle scientific errors.

insights.claim: More advanced LLMs no longer make the kinds of mistakes, like fabricated references, that free models made, so the forgery's failure mode may not persist.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Current detection advantage is temporary.
insights.quote: more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making

themes.theme: Detection arms race and peer-review overload

insights.claim: IEEE's publishing-ethics director expects detection tools built today may not work against tomorrow's AI-created papers.
insights.speaker: Luigi Longobardi
insights.so_what: Detection is a losing cat-and-mouse game; structural fixes are needed.
insights.quote: It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow

insights.claim: Peer review was already near breaking point before ubiquitous AI, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022, driven by publish-or-perish incentives and paper mills.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: AI amplifies an incentive problem rather than creating it.
insights.locator: Even before AI tools became ubiquitous

insights.claim: IEEE Access receives about 60,000 submissions a year and accepts about 20% (about 12,000), and the average number of reviewer invitations needed per article has risen 50% since 2018.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Volunteer reviewer capacity is the binding constraint in publishing.

insights.claim: Retraction Watch's cofounder frames AI as an accelerant on existing fire: publish-or-perish is the kindling and paper mills are the gasoline.
insights.speaker: Ivan Oransky
insights.so_what: Fixes must target incentives, not just AI tooling.
insights.quote: What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.

insights.claim: Oransky suggests the flood of AI slop could, optimistically, force first-principles reform of scientific publishing.
insights.speaker: Ivan Oransky
insights.so_what: Crisis may catalyze structural publishing reform.
insights.quote: maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level

insights.claim: Post-publication review on PubPeer and Retraction Watch is entirely volunteer-led, and even Ivan Oransky has found fabricated references attributed to himself.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: The last lines of defense are unpaid and overstretched.
insights.locator: Even the people who track problems

insights.claim: A wave of autonomous research systems, including FARS, AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher and DeepScientist, can go from a single prompt to literature review, experiments and a full paper with no further human input; LabClaw links to autonomous wet labs for tasks such as drug discovery.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Automated science is moving from digital-only into physical labs.
insights.locator: Often with just a single prompt

insights.claim: Analemma's FARS generated 166 papers in 417 hours; Analemma, a Singapore startup, was acquired by Baidu during reporting and the online FARS service was discontinued.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Big Tech is buying autonomous-research capability.
insights.quote: FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma.

insights.claim: FARS is an agentic orchestration system with four specialized agents for ideation, planning, experimentation and writing, drawing on any open- or closed-source LLM via a compute cluster.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Value lies in orchestration, not a proprietary model.

insights.claim: In the experiment FARS produced a research proposal in 21 minutes, ran the computational experiment overnight, and wrote a submission-ready paper in 2 hours.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Research cycle time collapses from months to about a day.
insights.locator: Round 2: Using an AI Science Engine

insights.claim: The FARS paper had no fake references but would still have been rejected by IEEE Access for heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints, likely reflecting the AI's data access, plus figure artifacts like a nonsense label 'lhewl'.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: AI-generated real research has new, subtler tells.

insights.claim: Papers from an AI Scientist system and from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review at the International Conference on Learning Representations in 2025.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Machine-authored research is already clearing top-venue review.

insights.claim: As autonomous research systems scale output, the author predicts a 'tsunami' that will threaten current scientific publishing processes.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: Publisher volume and review economics will break.
insights.quote: the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process

themes.theme: Future of the paper and trust infrastructure

insights.claim: Analemma argues the paper will cede its role as the unit of knowledge to a living knowledge graph of human and machine contributions, with automated reproducibility, statistics and novelty checks and humans judging significance.
insights.speaker: Xiwen Su
insights.so_what: Publishing could shift from journals to graph-based knowledge platforms.
insights.quote: FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge

insights.claim: IEEE Access is already automating triage of author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submissions and reference validity, and uses AI semantic search to match reviewers.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Publishers are adopting AI integrity tooling as a core function.

insights.claim: Mahoney argues AI should not be banned in research and that the key question is whether work can be trusted and reproduced, keeping humans at the wheel.
insights.speaker: Jenny Mahoney
insights.so_what: Reproducibility, not authorship origin, becomes the gating criterion.
insights.quote: The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?

insights.claim: Longobardi proposes provenance verification at the source, such as institutions linking lab equipment to blockchain-based trust markers proving who generated which data and when.
insights.speaker: Luigi Longobardi
insights.so_what: Opens a market for research-provenance and lab-data attestation tools.

insights.claim: Early provenance efforts exist: Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces departments assign unique IDs and QR codes to every sample, and University of Southampton chemistry rolled out electronic lab notebooks.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
entities: Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces
insights.so_what: Lab-data traceability is becoming an integrity tool.

insights.claim: The author concludes that deciding what counts as legitimate science may become harder than detecting outright fraud.
insights.speaker: Benjamin Skuse
insights.so_what: The definitional problem outlasts the detection problem.
insights.quote: deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud
